1.title: Level 1 - Foundations
1.blurb: Clear basics. Spot obvious false comfort.

variants.text: A programmer can skip reading the whole ticket if the title sounds familiar.
Before coding, a programmer should be able to say in one sentence what "done" looks like.
If a ticket is vague, guessing and coding fast is better than asking a question.
Re-reading the ticket before marking work finished can catch a requirement that was missed.
Acceptance notes in a ticket are optional suggestions rather than part of the request.
Running your own code once before handing it over is a basic duty.
If the code compiles with no errors, it has been tested.
A fix is not finished until you have tried the exact case that was reported broken.
Testing is someone else's job, so a programmer need not check anything.
Trying an empty or missing input is a normal part of checking your own work.
Short cryptic variable names save time and are fine in shared code.
Clear names let the next reader understand code without asking the author.
Code is read far more often than it is written, so readability matters.
A comment is always better than renaming a confusing variable.
Only the original author needs to understand the code they wrote.
Saving work in version control with a clear message helps teammates see what changed.
Committing a whole day's work as one commit named "stuff" is good practice.
Passwords can be committed to the repository if the repository is private.
Pulling the latest changes before you start avoids many avoidable conflicts.
A commit message should say what changed and why, not just "update".
Putting a password directly in the code is fine for a quick prototype that might ship.
Emailing a production key to a colleague is safe if you delete the email afterwards.
Secrets belong in a secure store or private settings, not in source files.
If a key is accidentally committed, it should be treated as exposed and replaced.
Removing a leaked key from the latest commit makes it safe again.
Asking a teammate after being stuck for a reasonable time is professional, not weak.
When asking for help, sharing the exact error message makes the answer faster.
Struggling alone for days without telling anyone shows dedication.
Saying "it doesn't work" is enough for a helper to diagnose the problem.
Saying what you already tried saves the helper from repeating it.
An error message can usually be ignored if the program keeps running.
The first lines of an error report often point to where the problem started.
Catching an error and doing nothing is a good way to keep users happy.
A good error message tells the user what went wrong and what they can do next.
Errors should be recorded with enough context to find the cause later.
Code copied from the internet should be understood before it goes into a product.
Code found online is free for any use with no license concerns.
Pasted code from an unknown source can carry security flaws.
If copied code works on your machine, it is safe to ship.
Copying a block from a competitor's project is fine if you rename the variables.
An estimate is a best guess with uncertainty, not a promise carved in stone.
Breaking a task into smaller pieces usually makes an estimate more reliable.
Quoting the best possible case is the honest way to give an estimate.
Telling the team early that a task will run late is better than hiding it.
Quietly working extra nights is the best answer to an optimistic estimate.
Personal style beats team style because good programmers know best.
Skipping the formatting rules is fine when the code works.
Following the team's agreed conventions makes everyone's code easier to review.
Review comments are personal attacks and should be argued every time.
When a reviewer points out a real bug, the right response is to fix it and say thanks.

2.title: Level 2 - Trade-offs
2.blurb: Two good-looking options; only one is sound.

slots.theme: Speed versus quality on a deadline

variants.text: When a deadline is tight, cutting scope is usually safer than cutting testing.
Skipping checks to hit a date is fine because quality can be added later for free.
Shipping a smaller working feature on time beats shipping a larger broken one.
A deadline justifies leaving known data-loss bugs as long as the demo looks good.
Telling the owner what will be left out lets them choose, instead of you quietly choosing for them.

slots.theme: Fixing the symptom versus the cause

variants.text: A quick patch that hides a crash is as good as finding why it crashes.
A temporary workaround is acceptable if it is labeled and the real cause is tracked.
Once the error message disappears, the underlying bug is gone.
Asking "why did that happen" several times in a row often leads to the true cause.
Fixing only the one failing customer record solves a bug that comes from bad logic.
Improving old code in small tested steps is usually less risky than rewriting it from scratch.
A full rewrite is always faster because old code has nothing worth keeping.
Rewriting is safe because nobody ever relied on the old code's odd behavior.
Ugly old code often contains fixes for real problems that a rewrite may forget.
Before changing messy code, add a test that records what it does today.

slots.theme: Use a library or write it yourself

variants.text: Writing your own password protection is better than a trusted library because you understand it fully.
For well-solved problems like date handling, a mature library is usually the sounder choice.
Adding a tiny library for one trivial function has a cost, since it must be kept updated.
A popular library with years of unfixed security issues is safe because many people use it.
Using a library means you no longer need to understand what it does with your data.
A comment explaining why a strange choice was made is more useful than one repeating what the line does.
Renaming a confusing function can remove the need for a comment.
Every line should have a comment so nobody is ever confused.
Comments never go out of date, so they are safer than clear code.
An outdated comment that contradicts the code can mislead worse than no comment at all.
One huge change covering many topics is easier to review because the reviewer sees everything.
Splitting work into small changes just creates paperwork with no benefit.
Small focused changes are easier to review and easier to undo if something breaks.
Mixing a bug fix with unrelated cleanup makes it harder to tell which change caused a problem.
Reviewers catch more problems in a 3,000-line change than in a 100-line one.
Measuring where a program is slow before tuning it prevents wasted effort.
Making every function as fast as possible from day one is the mark of a good programmer.
Clear simple code is usually the right first version unless a real speed problem is shown.
When users report a slow page, guessing the cause and rewriting that part is the best first step.
Speed never matters, so a programmer should never look at performance.
Hiding errors from users is always kinder than showing a failure.
Stopping with a clear failure is better than continuing with wrong data.
Returning a default value like zero when a lookup fails is always harmless.
Showing users a friendly message while recording full details for developers balances both needs.
A payment step that cannot confirm success should report uncertainty rather than claim success.
Hardcoding a server address in ten places is quicker and just as safe in the long run.
Making every single value configurable is always better with no downside.
Values that differ between test and live systems belong in settings, not scattered through code.
A setting nobody documents is just as easy to run as a documented one.
Many undocumented options can make a system harder to run than a few sensible defaults.
A little repetition can be better than a confusing shared helper built too early.
When the same logic is copied three times and keeps changing together, sharing it is sensible.
Any two similar-looking blocks should always be merged into one flexible function.
A shared function with many on/off switches can be harder to understand than two simple ones.
Copy-pasting a block and changing a few words is the fastest safe way every time.

3.title: Level 3 - Failure modes
3.blurb: What breaks under load, time, or bad incentives.

variants.text: If it runs on your laptop, it will run the same way in production.
Differences in versions or settings between machines are a common reason code fails after release.
Production problems that do not appear locally must be user mistakes.
Writing down how to set up and run the project helps others reproduce the same behavior.
Testing only on the newest computer you own proves it works for all users.
A name field may receive empty text, very long text, or accented letters, and code should cope.
Users always enter data in the format the form designer imagined.
A report that works for ten rows may fail or crawl at ten million.
A number typed into a text box is always a valid number.
A person with a single name can break code that assumes every name has two parts.
Storing local time with no time zone is fine for a service used across countries.
Daylight saving changes can make some local times occur twice or not at all.
A date like 03/04/2025 can be read as March 4 or April 3 depending on the reader.
Adding 24 hours always lands on the same clock time the next day.
The clocks on all servers are always perfectly identical.
Loading every record into memory at once can crash a program when data grows.
A page that is fast with test data will be equally fast with a year of real data.
Retrying a failed request instantly and forever is a safe way to be reliable.
Retries without a limit or delay can overload a service that is already struggling.
Limits such as page size and timeouts protect a system from runaway requests.
Updating every library the moment a new version appears is always risk free.
Never updating libraries is safe because untouched code cannot break.
A library whose version is not fixed can change under you and break a build that worked yesterday.
A small package you rely on can be removed or abandoned by its owner.
Dependencies are the vendor's problem, so a programmer need not know what the project relies on.
An empty "catch" block can hide a problem for months.
When a background job fails with no alert, nobody may notice until customers complain.
No complaints means no failures.
Recording an error with no detail is enough to diagnose it later.
Failures that stay silent are more dangerous than ones that crash loudly.
Praise for the fastest fix encourages careful work.
Rewarding only speed can push people to skip tests and create more incidents.
A hotfix pushed at night without review is safe because it is small.
A quick hotfix should be followed by a proper fix so the shortcut does not become permanent.
Tiny changes can still break production, so a second pair of eyes is worth the minute it costs.
Two users saving the same record at the same moment can overwrite each other's work.
If code works for one user at a time, it works for many at once.
Checking "is there stock?" and then deducting it as separate steps can sell the same item twice.
Bugs that appear only sometimes are usually random luck and can be ignored.
Adding a short pause to the code is a proper permanent fix for timing bugs.
When code is copied, a bug fixed in one copy may remain in the others.
Searching for similar code after fixing a bug helps find the same mistake elsewhere.
Once the reported spot is fixed, every other place with the same mistake is fixed too.
Keeping one source for a rule, like a tax rate, prevents copies from disagreeing.
Different tax rates on different screens are a minor cosmetic issue.
A TODO comment from three years ago still guarantees the work will happen.
Unused code does no harm because it is never run.
Old unused code can mislead readers and sometimes still runs through a forgotten path.
Turning off a feature by commenting out half of it is a clean way to retire it.
Removing code that is truly dead lowers confusion, and version control keeps the history.

4.title: Level 4 - Precedents & traps
4.blurb: Industry-familiar traps dressed as best practice.

variants.text: High test coverage can still miss bugs if the tests do not check the right outcomes.
A project with 100 percent coverage cannot have bugs.
A test that runs code but checks nothing raises the coverage number without proving anything.
Coverage percentage is the best single measure of software quality.
Meaningful tests on risky areas beat chasing a number across trivial code.
A programmer who writes more lines each week is clearly more productive.
Deleting code while keeping behavior the same can be real progress.
Counting commits per day is a fair way to rank programmers.
Measuring output by volume invites people to pad work rather than solve problems.
A long solution is proof of effort and therefore of quality.
A clever one-line trick that nobody can read is a maintenance cost.
Dense clever code shows seniority and should be preferred.
Reviewers who ask for simpler code are just slowing the team down.
Plain code that a new teammate understands in a minute is usually the better choice.
If you must be clever for speed, explain the trick in a short comment.

slots.theme: If it ain't broke, don't touch it

variants.text: "If it ain't broke, don't touch it" means never update anything, including security fixes.
Leaving old software unpatched can turn a working system into a security hole.
Code that works today may sit on an outdated platform that will soon stop being supported.
Old code that nobody touches has no risk, so it needs no owner.
Keeping the oldest version of every tool forever is the most stable policy.
A test where everything is faked may pass while the real system fails.
Mixing a few real integration checks with fast isolated tests gives better confidence.
If all tests use fakes and pass, the connections between parts are proven.
Faking every outside piece is always the best testing style.
A fake that returns what the code expects can hide a mismatch with the real service.
A programmer who fixes everything alone overnight is the ideal team member.
Only one person knowing how a system works is a sign of strength.
Relying on one hero for fixes creates a risk when that person is away or tired.
Sharing knowledge through notes and reviews reduces the risk of one person being essential.
Heroic effort in every crisis shows the process is healthy.
A newer tool is worth adopting only if it solves a problem the team actually has.
Using the newest framework is always best because it is the future.
Choosing a tool nobody on the team knows adds learning cost and risk.
A framework popular on social media is therefore proven for your project.
Staying on old tools forever is always wiser than ever changing.
A passing build means the feature does what the customer wanted.
A green build only shows that the checks that exist have passed.
If the pipeline is green, looking over the change by eye is unnecessary.
A build that turns green after tests were deleted or skipped deserves suspicion.
Trying the actual feature in a realistic setting adds confidence beyond automated checks.
Well-named code means no one ever needs any documentation.
Documentation is a waste because code never needs a guide.
Code can show what happens but often not why a decision was made.
A README that does not match the project is still helpful because it exists.
A short note on how to run and set up the project saves new teammates hours.
Commented-out code kept "just in case" clutters files and confuses readers.
Version control already remembers old code, so deleting it is usually safe.
Leaving big blocks of disabled code is the safest habit.
A reader cannot tell whether commented-out code is important or forgotten.
Deleting old code always loses it forever.

5.title: Level 5 - Edge judgment
5.blurb: Subtle cases where polite process still fails the user.

slots.theme: When the ticket would cause harm

variants.text: If the ticket says to do it, the programmer has no responsibility to mention a harm.
A programmer who sees that a requested change could mislead users should raise it before building it.
Following the ticket exactly is always the same as serving the customer.
Raising a concern with a clear example is more useful than refusing silently or complying silently.
Building the feature quietly and hoping nobody notices the problem is a neutral choice.
A bug noticed outside your task should be reported or ticketed even if you do not fix it.
Unrelated bugs are none of your business, so staying silent is correct.
Slipping a large unrelated fix into your change makes review harder, so mention it separately.
If you saw a bug, assuming someone else already reported it is safe.
A short, clear note about where you saw the problem helps whoever picks it up.
A quick approval from a trusted reviewer means the author needs to check nothing more.
Reviewers see only the changed lines, so the author still owns thinking about side effects.
A reviewer approving at speed may simply be trusting you, which is a reason to be more careful.
A review approval transfers all blame for later bugs to the reviewer.
An approval in a review means the change was tested.
A test that fails randomly should be fixed or removed with a note, not rerun until it passes.
Rerunning a flaky test until green is a harmless habit.
Flaky tests are noise, so the team can ignore all red results.
If people learn to ignore red builds, a real failure can slip through.
A flaky test can sometimes point to a real timing bug in the code.
A tight deadline is a good reason to skip a required security review.
Skipping a login check on an internal tool is fine because only staff can reach it.
Even small features that handle personal data deserve the same care as large ones.
If a security step truly cannot be done in time, the risk should be put in writing for the owner to decide.
A security flaw only matters after someone has been caught exploiting it.
Writing customers' passwords or card numbers into logs is dangerous even if the logs are internal.
Logs are often copied to many tools and kept for long, so what goes in can spread.
Logs are private, so anything can be written to them.
Hiding sensitive values in logs makes debugging impossible.
A record ID usually helps debugging about as well as a person's full details, with less risk.

slots.theme: Shipping with a known minor bug

variants.text: A known bug can be left out of the release notes if it seems minor.
Shipping with a known bug should be a decision made by the owner who knows about it.
A bug that affects only a few users never needs to be told to the owner.
A minor bug in a billing screen can be worse than a major bug on a rarely used page.
Recording the known issue with steps to reproduce makes it easier to fix later.
Disagreeing with a senior colleague is fine if you give a specific reason and respect the decision made.
A senior person's approach should always be followed silently because seniority equals correctness.
Bringing evidence such as a test or an example persuades better than an opinion.
After losing a technical argument, quietly doing it your way is acceptable.
Complaining about the decision to other teammates is a good way to be heard.
Before changing code nobody understands, writing tests that capture current behavior reduces risk.
Asking people who used the system what it is supposed to do is a good starting point.
Confusing code is a sign it can be safely deleted and replaced this week.
Changing one small thing at a time makes inherited code easier to trust.
If the previous owner has left, nothing about the code can be learned.

slots.theme: Tests pass but the user's problem remains

variants.text: If all tests pass, the user's original complaint is definitely solved.
Closing the ticket is the same as helping the customer.
Checking with the person who reported the problem confirms the fix actually helped.
A fix that works for the sample in the ticket works for every similar case.
A programmer who tries the fix as the user would may find the problem is still there.

1.title: Level 1 - Foundations
1.blurb: Clear basics. Spot obvious false comfort.

variants.text: Automated tests are a luxury that slows a team down with no benefit.
Automated tests let an engineer change code and quickly learn whether something else broke.
A feature with no tests is safe because nobody has complained yet.
A bug that was found and fixed should get a test so it does not quietly return.
One person clicking around before release can replace all automated checks forever.
Code review helps catch mistakes and spreads knowledge across the team.
Code review exists mainly to prove who is the better engineer.
A review comment should be about the code, not about the person who wrote it.
Small changes never need review.
Authors should explain what changed and why in the description so reviewers can help effectively.
Engineers build best when they never speak to the people who will use the product.
Knowing who uses a feature and why helps an engineer make better design choices.
Confirming your understanding of a request with the requester prevents building the wrong thing.
A written request always means exactly what the writer intended, so questions are wasted time.
Requirements never change once a project has started.
Releasing small changes often makes problems easier to find than releasing a giant batch rarely.
Releasing everything once every six months is the safest approach.
A release with no way to go back is fine if the team feels confident.
Being able to undo a release quickly lowers the risk of releasing.
Releasing early in the work week leaves time to fix issues before the weekend.
Logs are only for people who enjoy reading text files.
The more a system logs, the better, so it should log everything including passwords.
Useful logs say what happened, when, and which request was involved without exposing secrets.
When something fails at 2 a.m., logs are often the only witness.
Logging is unnecessary if the code is correct.
Writing down why a design was chosen helps future engineers avoid repeating old debates.
A short decision note is better than relying on someone's memory of a meeting.
Documentation is only for large companies.
A decision made in a hallway chat needs no record because everyone heard it.
Notes on how to run, release and troubleshoot a service help whoever is on call.
A copy of data on the same disk counts as a full backup.
A backup is only useful if it can actually be restored.
Using cloud storage means backups are never needed.
Important data should be backed up on a regular schedule.
Keeping at least one backup in a separate location protects against a site-wide problem.
Engineers should collect only the personal data the feature really needs.
Keeping all user data forever is harmless and might be useful someday.
Personal data in a test environment should be masked or replaced with fake data.
Storing passwords in plain text is acceptable if the database is behind a firewall.
Pasting a customer's records into a public chat to get quick help is fine.
Giving honest status updates, including bad news, helps the team plan.
Saying "blocked, need X from Y" is more useful than going quiet.
Reporting "almost done" for weeks is a helpful way to avoid worry.
Updating the ticket when scope or timing changes keeps everyone informed.
Status updates are a waste of time for engineers.
Everyone should fix problems in other teams' code without telling them.
Pushing straight to the main branch with no checks is fine if you are experienced.
Agreeing on how branches, reviews and releases work reduces collisions in a shared codebase.
Leaving broken code on the main branch until someone else notices is acceptable.
When you break the build, fixing or reverting it quickly respects your teammates' time.

2.title: Level 2 - Trade-offs
2.blurb: Two good-looking options; only one is sound.

variants.text: Buying a ready product for a common need like sending email often beats building it, since the team can focus on what makes the business different.
Building everything in-house is always cheaper because there are no license fees.
A bought product still has costs in setup, connection to other systems, and dependence on the vendor.
Once you buy a product, nobody on the team needs to understand how it works.
If a need is the heart of what sets the business apart, building it in-house is often worth the effort.
Splitting a small app into many services always makes it faster to build.
One deployable application is often simpler to run for a small team than many small services.
Services are better because each one never needs to talk to the others.
Splitting into services adds network calls and more things that can fail.
A big application should never be split regardless of its size or the number of teams.
Spending some time each cycle on cleanup can keep new features from slowing down later.
Messy code never costs anything, so features should always come first.
Stopping all feature work for a year to clean code is the standard sound approach.
Mess that slows every change is worth cleaning sooner than mess in code nobody touches.
Explaining cleanup in terms of customer impact helps non-engineers agree to it.
Accepting any input without checks is friendlier and so always better.
Checking input at the edge of the system stops bad data from spreading inside.
Too-strict rules, such as rejecting valid phone formats, can block real customers.
Checking input only in the browser is enough since users cannot bypass it.
An error message that says only "invalid" is the best way to guide users.
Automated checks cost time up front but make later releases faster and safer.
Slow checks that people skip give less protection than fast checks that always run.
Removing checks to speed up the pipeline is always a sound trade.
A pipeline that takes two hours is fine because engineers can work on something else meanwhile.
Running quick checks on every change and heavy ones less often balances speed and safety.
Caching is always safe because showing slightly older data never matters.
Avoiding caches is always better because fresh data is the only goal.
Caching speeds up repeated reads but can show outdated information.
For data like a bank balance, showing stale values can be unacceptable.
A cache never needs a plan for when its contents should be refreshed.
Keeping unfinished work behind an on/off switch lets teams merge often and release when ready.
A branch kept apart for three months merges painlessly at the end.
Old on/off switches that are never removed make code harder to understand.
A feature switch removes the need to test the switched-off code.
A switch left on in production for a year needs no further attention.

slots.theme: Doing work now or in the background

variants.text: Doing a slow task while the user waits is always simplest and therefore best.
Sending a confirmation email in the background keeps the page fast for the user.
Work moved to the background can never fail, so no monitoring is needed.
Background tasks need a plan for retries and for telling someone when they keep failing.
Giving the user a clear "we're working on it" message beats a frozen screen.
Letting every team pick its own tools never causes any cost.
One mandatory tool set for every team is always best regardless of their needs.
Common tools make it easier to move engineers between teams and share fixes.
A rule that can never be questioned keeps standards healthy.
A good standard has a clear route for exceptions when a team has a real reason.
Releasing a simple version to learn from real users can beat polishing for months.
A first release should still be safe with data and security even if features are few.
"Minimum viable" means skipping login protection since it can be added later.
Learning from early use can reveal that some planned features were not needed.
A first release should include every feature on the wish list.

3.title: Level 3 - Failure modes
3.blurb: What breaks under load, time, or bad incentives.

variants.text: If a release passed testing, a way to undo it is unnecessary.
A release with no tested way back can turn a small mistake into a long outage.
Rolling back is a sign of failure, so teams should avoid it.
Database changes can make rollbacks harder, so they need extra planning.
Practicing a rollback for the first time during a real outage is a fine plan.
Without monitoring, customers may discover an outage before the team does.
If the server is running, the service is working.
Alerts should point to something a person can act on.
Checking the system by hand once a day is as good as automatic alerts.
Measuring errors and slow responses shows problems that "up or down" checks miss.
If another service is slow, it cannot affect your service.
Waiting forever on a slow partner can tie up your own resources and bring you down too.
Setting time limits on outside calls helps contain a partner's problems.
Retrying a struggling service harder will help it recover.
Outside services can be assumed to be always available.
A change that locks a big table can freeze the whole application at busy times.
A data change that took one second on test data will take one second in production.
Running a large data change at peak hours is fine if you warn people.
Doing risky changes in small steps allows stopping before damage spreads.
Taking a backup before a large data change gives you a way to recover.
More alerts always mean a safer system.
Muting a noisy alert forever is a good fix.
When people get too many false alarms, they may miss the one that matters.
Alerts that fire often but need no action should be tuned or removed.
Engineers should respond to every alert the same way regardless of severity.
If only one person can release, vacations and illness become delivery risks.
Documenting and sharing the release steps reduces that risk.
Having one expert is efficient and has no downsides.
A release process that lives only in one person's head is stable because it is consistent.
Having a second person do the release alongside the expert is a good way to spread skill.
A system that handles 100 users will scale to 100,000 without changes.
Some limits, like the number of database connections, only show up when traffic grows.
Load testing is unnecessary if the code is clean.
Testing with realistic amounts of data catches problems that small samples hide.
Knowing the expected peak use before launch helps decide what to test.
A backup that has never been restored might not work when it is needed.
A backup job reporting "success" proves the data can be recovered.
Practicing a restore on a schedule shows how long recovery really takes.
Having backups means recovery time does not need to be thought about.
Only the people who set up backups need to know how to restore.
Measuring engineers by tickets closed can push them to split work into many tiny tickets.
Closing a ticket does not prove the customer's problem is solved.
A high ticket count proves a team is healthy.
Looking at outcomes like fewer incidents tells more than counting completed items.
Measures that are easy to count are always the most meaningful ones.
Test and production can differ in many settings without causing surprises.
Fixing a setting by hand on one live server is a harmless quick fix.
Manual changes on live servers can make environments differ in ways nobody remembers.
If production works, nobody needs a record of how it is set up.
Keeping settings in version control helps rebuild an environment the same way.

Rewriting a working system from scratch often takes longer than planned.

The right amount of caution depends on how costly and reversible a mistake is.

A trial with the customer's own data and users is stronger evidence.
Asking to see the product handle a messy case helps test a demo.
A reference customer proves the product will fit any other customer.
A reference customer in a similar situation is more informative than one in a different situation.
Vendors usually choose references that are happy, so they show the best case.
Reference calls always give a balanced view.
A big brand name as a customer guarantees quality.
A fixed price on unclear scope tends to lead to disputes about what is included.
Fixed price works best when the scope is well defined.
Fixed price always protects the customer from cost increases.
A fixed price quote removes the need to define scope.
Splitting discovery from delivery lets the scope become clear before the price is fixed.
Anything the customer wants can be done by changing settings.
Calling custom code "configuration" makes it easier to maintain.
Real configuration is supported by the vendor, while custom code is not.
The difference matters because custom code can break at upgrade time.
Customers do not care about how a change is made.
Winning a feature checklist does not mean the product fits how the customer works.
The product with the most ticks in the checklist is the best choice.
Asking how well each feature works matters more than whether it exists.
A checklist covers everything that matters in a purchase.
Features listed as "partial" can be treated as "yes".

slots.theme: Lift and shift to the cloud

variants.text: Moving existing systems to the cloud unchanged always saves money.
Moving systems unchanged can leave the customer paying cloud prices for inefficient designs.
Lift and shift is always the fastest path to modernization.
It may be a sensible first step when a data center contract is ending.
Planning improvements after the move can capture savings later.
Vendor benchmark numbers always predict real-world performance.
A benchmark published by the vendor is independent.
Benchmarks are run under conditions chosen to suit the vendor's product.
A benchmark result transfers to any workload.
Testing with the customer's own workload gives a more meaningful answer.
A single training session does not guarantee people will use the system well.
Training works best with practice, support and follow-up over time.
Once users have been trained, adoption is assured.
Hearing from users after launch shows what training missed.
Training budget is the first thing to cut with little risk.

5.title: Level 5 - Edge judgment
5.blurb: Subtle cases where polite process still fails the user.

slots.theme: The solution would not solve the problem

variants.text: If the customer asks for it, the solutions architect should simply provide it.
If the requested solution will not solve the stated problem, the architect should say so.
Raising a concern about a request is unprofessional.
Explaining the gap with an example helps the customer see it.
Delivering a solution known not to work is acceptable because the customer chose it.

slots.theme: Losing a deal by being honest

variants.text: Being honest about a poor fit may lose a sale but protects trust over time.
An architect should stay quiet about a misfit to protect the quarter's numbers.
A customer who was told the truth may return when the fit is better.
Competitors will not mention the same weakness, so it is safe to ignore.
Recommending a different path that really serves the customer builds reputation.
A solutions architect should never admit a competitor is a better fit.
When a competitor fits better, saying so respectfully can preserve the relationship.
Offering to help with the part where your product fits can still be valuable.
Criticizing the competitor is the best way to show confidence.
Hiding the competitor's strengths is a normal part of the job.
A proposal built on an assumption the customer never confirmed carries hidden risk.
If the customer says nothing about an assumption, it is confirmed.
Assumptions can be left out of the document to keep it short.
Asking the customer to confirm key assumptions in writing reduces disputes.
Flagging which assumptions affect price makes the proposal more honest.
Using real customer data in a demo environment is fine because it is only a demo.
Copying a customer's data to a laptop for convenience is harmless.
Real customer data in a demo or test needs the same protection as in production.
Using fake data that looks real is a safer way to demonstrate.
Data that is loaded temporarily needs no deletion afterwards.
A new requirement after sign-off should be handled through the agreed change process.
Explaining the effect on cost and time of a late requirement helps the customer decide.
Late requirements should always be absorbed to keep the customer happy.
Saying no to every late requirement is always the right response.

A limitation can be left out of the contract if it seems unlikely to matter.
A limitation that affects the customer's use should be stated clearly, even if it is awkward.
If the customer does not ask about a limitation, there is no duty to mention it.

A customer's own architect may know the environment better and deserves to be heard.
When a customer's architect disagrees, the solutions architect should push harder.
Understanding the reason for the disagreement can improve the design.
The customer's architect is a blocker who should be avoided.
Going over their head to their manager is the best way to resolve it.
A story told to a customer should be true and approved by the reference customer.
A slightly exaggerated claim can still damage trust and create legal risk.
A small exaggeration is acceptable if it helps the customer see the value.
If you are unsure whether a claim is accurate, checking it first is better than guessing.

Risks that were discussed only in private conversations need not be handed over.
Keeping known risks from the delivery team avoids worrying them.
Passing known risks to the delivery team in writing helps them plan.
A handoff is complete when the contract is signed.
